rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What is refractive index?
rows.originalBack: n = c/v for light in the medium.
accept: Refractive index equals the speed of light in vacuum divided by its speed in the medium: n=c/v.
reject: Refractive index is n=v/c, the speed in the medium divided by the vacuum speed.
Refractive index is n=cv, the product of both speeds.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: When can total internal reflection occur?
rows.originalBack: Light travels from higher to lower refractive index.
accept: Total internal reflection is possible when light travels from a higher-index medium towards a lower-index medium at an angle greater than the critical angle.
reject: Total internal reflection occurs when light travels from a lower refractive index into a higher one.
Total internal reflection occurs below the critical angle rather than above it.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What causes an optical fibre to guide light?
rows.originalBack: Total internal reflection at its boundary.
accept: Repeated total internal reflection at the core-cladding boundary guides light through an optical fibre.
reject: Light is guided because the core absorbs all rays that hit its boundary.
An optical fibre guides light by repeated refraction out of the core into the cladding.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What happens to light wavelength on entering a higher-index medium?
rows.originalBack: It decreases.
accept: Entering a higher-index medium reduces the wavelength because speed falls while frequency stays constant.
reject: The wavelength increases when light enters a higher-index medium.
Light frequency increases so the wavelength remains unchanged as it enters the medium.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What is the critical-angle equation for air outside a material?
rows.originalBack: sin c = 1/n.
accept: For light travelling from a medium of refractive index n to air, sin of the critical angle equals 1/n.
reject: For a medium-air interface, sine of the critical angle equals n.
The critical angle is equal to n degrees regardless of the material.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What is the derived SI unit of resistivity?
rows.originalBack: Ohm metre (Ω m).
accept: The SI derived unit of resistivity is the ohm metre, symbol Ω m.
reject: Resistivity is measured in ohms per metre, Ω/m.
The resistivity SI unit is the siemens per metre, S/m.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: Which graph is used to find a cell's emf and internal resistance?
rows.originalBack: Terminal p.d. V against current I.
accept: Plot terminal potential difference V vertically against current I horizontally; the intercept gives emf and the gradient is minus internal resistance.
reject: Plot current on the y-axis against voltage on x, giving emf as the vertical intercept.
Plot terminal potential difference against time to calculate the internal resistance from its gradient.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: How is wire cross-sectional area obtained from diameter d?
rows.originalBack: A = πd²/4.
accept: The circular area of a wire of measured diameter d is π(d/2)², equal to πd²/4.
reject: Wire area from its diameter is πd² without dividing by four.
Wire area is πd/4, omitting the square of diameter.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What does the gradient of resistance against wire length give?
rows.originalBack: ρ/A, for a wire of constant cross-section.
accept: For a uniform wire, the gradient of resistance plotted against length is resistivity divided by cross-sectional area, ρ/A.
reject: The slope of resistance against wire length equals A/ρ.
The resistance versus length gradient equals ρ multiplied by A.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: Why should current not be left flowing unnecessarily in a cell experiment?
rows.originalBack: Heating and changing cell conditions can alter measurements.
accept: Switch the current off between readings to reduce heating and prevent the cell's conditions changing during the experiment.
reject: Leave current running between readings to prevent temperature changes.
Heating a cell continuously removes its internal resistance and improves the readings.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What does gradient of a stress (y) against strain (x) graph give?
rows.originalBack: Young modulus E in the linear elastic region: E = stress ÷ strain (in Pa).
accept: In the straight-line elastic part, the stress-y versus strain-x gradient equals the Young modulus E in pascals.
reject: The slope of stress plotted against strain equals 1/E.
Young modulus is the gradient only after permanent plastic deformation begins.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: For a stress–strain graph, when does the gradient give Young modulus?
rows.originalBack: In the straight-line elastic region: E = Δstress/Δstrain.
accept: Only in the linear elastic region does stress divided by strain, or Δstress/Δstrain, give Young modulus.
reject: The Young modulus is found from gradient in the plastic region after the yield point.
Young modulus from a stress-strain plot equals change in strain divided by change in stress.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What is the ultimate tensile stress?
rows.originalBack: Maximum tensile stress before breaking.
accept: Ultimate tensile stress is the largest tensile stress the material reaches on the stress-strain curve.
reject: Ultimate tensile stress is the strain, not the stress, at fracture.
Ultimate tensile stress is always the same as the elastic limit stress.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: A 20 N force acts at 30° to a 0.50 m lever arm. Find its moment about the pivot.
rows.originalBack: M = Fr sinθ = 20×0.50×sin30° = 5.0 N m.
accept: Use the perpendicular component: moment = 20 N × 0.50 m × sin30° = 5.0 N m.
reject: Moment equals 20 times 0.50 times cos30°, or about 8.7 N m.
The force is all perpendicular, so the moment equals 10 N m.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: Two equal opposite 15 N forces form a couple separated by 0.40 m. Find the moment.
rows.originalBack: Moment of the couple = Fd = 15×0.40 = 6.0 N m. Do not double it.
accept: The turning moment of this couple is one force times perpendicular separation, 15 N × 0.40 m = 6.0 N m.
reject: Double the two forces: this couple has moment 12 N m.
The couple moment is zero since the forces cancel as a resultant force.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: In the couple formula M = Fd, what does distance d represent?
rows.originalBack: d is the perpendicular separation between the forces' lines of action. Use just one F; don't double Fd.
accept: In M=Fd for a couple, d is the shortest perpendicular distance between the lines of action of the two forces.
reject: The couple distance d is the object's displacement during rotation.
The couple separation d is measured along the force direction, not perpendicular to it.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: An object's kinetic energy rises from 5 J to 30 J. What is the net work done on it?
accept: Net work done equals the increase in kinetic energy, 30 minus 5 = positive 25 J.
reject: Net work equals 35 J because both kinetic energies are added.
Net work is negative 25 J even though the kinetic energy increases.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: A force parallel to motion rises linearly from 0 to 40 N across 2.0 m. Find work done.
rows.originalBack: Work = triangular area under F–s graph = ½×2.0×40 = 40 J.
accept: The work equals triangular area under force-distance graph, half times 2.0 metres times 40 newtons = 40 joules.
reject: The work is 80 joules using the rectangular area even though force rises linearly.
Work is 20 joules because only half the stated displacement matters.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: An engine exerts a 30 N force along the direction of travel at 4.0 m s⁻¹. Find power.
accept: Since force and velocity are parallel, P=Fv=30×4.0=120 watts.
reject: Power is force divided by speed, 30/4=7.5 watts.
Power is force plus speed, giving 34 watts.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: A device receives 150 J and transfers 60 J usefully. Calculate efficiency.
rows.originalBack: Efficiency = useful output/input = 60/150 = 0.40 = 40%.
accept: Efficiency equals useful output divided by total input: 60/150 = 0.40 or 40%.
reject: Efficiency is input over output, 150/60 = 250%.
Efficiency is 90% because subtracting 60 joules from 150 joules gives 90.
